'''Arikapú''' (also historically called '''Mashubi''') is an [[endangered language|endangered]] [[Yabutian languages|Yabutian]] language, historically spoken by the Arikapú people in the upper reaches of the [[Amazon basin]]. The language is moribund, with only two living speakers, and no one actively learning the language.<ref name="IPB2018"/><ref name="RV2010">{{cite journal |last1=Ribeiro |first1=Eduardo Rivail |last2=van der Voort |first2=Hein |title=Nimuendajú Was Right: The Inclusion of the Jabutí Language Family in the Macro-Jê Stock |journal=International Journal of American Linguistics |date=2010 |volume=76 |issue=4 |pages=517–570 |doi=10.1086/658056 |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/658056 |access-date=21 January 2026 |issn=0020-7071 |lang=en}}</ref> A bilingual Arikapú-Portuguese dictionary with approximately 1350 words has been compiled, along with a [[Latin script]] writing system for the language.<ref name=Vocab/>

==Speakers==
As of 2018, only two people still speak Arikapú. The language was more widely spoken by the Arikapú people, who lived in the Brazilian state of [[Rondônia]], along the upper reaches of the Rio Branco, a tributary of the [[Guaporé River]]. Beginning in the early 20th century, Brazilian colonization displaced the Arikapú people, with many of them moving downstream to work in rubber plantations.<ref name=IPB2018/>

The number of Arikapú speakers has been dropping over time. Prior to colonization, there were likely thousands of speakers. A 2007 study estimated less than 50 people still spoke Arikapú, and by 2015, the number of speakers was down to two. By 2018, the two known speakers were living in different [[Indigenous territory (Brazil)|Indigenous Territories]], with no one in the younger generations learning the language.<ref name=IPB2018/><ref name="Nikulin2020">{{cite thesis|last1=Nikulin |first1=Andrey |title=Proto-Macro-Jê: um estudo reconstrutivo |date=2020 |url=http://etnolinguistica.org/local--files/tese%3Anikulin-2020/Nikulin_2020_Proto-Macro-Je.pdf |access-date=21 January 2026 |language=pt,en |degree=PhD |publisher=University of Brasília}}</ref>{{rp|27}}<ref name=":0">Djeoromitxi, A. K. ''O fortalecimento da língua e cultura Djeromitxi a partir da for-mação dos professores''. 2015. 79 f. Monografia (Licenciatura em Educação Básica Intercultural) – Departamento de Educação Intercultural, Universidade Federal de Rondônia (câmpus de Ji-Paraná).</ref> Ethnic Arikapú people living in the Indigenous Territories now speak [[Tuparí language|Tuparí]], [[Makuráp language|Makuráp]], or [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]], and share aspects of their culture with the other peoples of the local Marico cultural complex.<ref name=IPB2018/>

==Classification==
Arikapú is closely related to the nearby [[Djeoromitxí language]], and the two languages are grouped together as the [[Yabutian languages|Yabutian (or Jabutí) languages]]. Though originally thought to be unrelated to other indigenous languages, they are likely a branch of the [[Macro-Jê languages|Macro-Jê language family]]. The linguistic differences between Arikapú and Djeoromitxí suggest that their speakers separated around 2,000 years ago, after moving from the east (where the other Macro-Jê languages are spoken). The Yabutian languages are the westernmost members of the Macro-Jê family.<ref name="IPB2018"/><ref name=RV2010/><ref name="Nikulin2020"/>{{rp|27}}

Historically, there have been some reports of a third language related to Arikapú, called Mashubi or Maxubí. These include a 1914 wordlist by explorer [[Percy Fawcett]], the earliest known documentation of any Jabutían language,<ref name="RV2010" /> and [[Čestmír Loukotka]]'s 1968 classification of South American languages.<ref name="Loukotka">{{cite book |last=Loukotka |first=Čestmír |author-link=Čestmír Loukotka |title=Classification of South American Indian languages |url=https://archive.org/details/classificationof0007louk |url-access=registration |publisher=UCLA Latin American Center |year=1968 |location=Los Angeles}}</ref>{{rp|99}} However, follow-up research suggests that this was an erroneous label; indigenous groups had never heard of Mashubi and the wordlist largely overlapped with Arikapú. As a result, it is now believed that Mashubi is not a separate language but an alternative name for Arikapú.<ref name=V2012>{{Cite journal |title=Whatever happened to Mashubi? Taking a new look at Fawcett's vocabulary |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/issue:vol4n1 |journal=Cadernos de Etnolingüística |issn=1946-7095 |access-date=2025-09-17 |volume=4 |number=1 |date=2012 |last=van der Voort |first=Hein}}</ref>

===Vowels===
Arikapú has fourteen vowels, with distinctions in vowel quality ([[Vowel height|height]], [[backness]]) and nasality. Eight are oral vowels, and six of them are [[Nasal vowel|nasalized]] versions of the oral vowels:<ref name="Voort2007">{{cite journal |last1=van der Voort |first1=Hein |title=Proto-Jabutí: um primeiro passo na reconstrução da língua ancestral dos Arikapú e Djeoromitxí |journal=Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi, Ciências Humanas |date=2007 |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=133-168 |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/artigo:voort-2007a |access-date=21 January 2026 |lang=pt}}</ref>{{rp|137}}

[[Minimal pair]]s exist between oral and nasal vowels. For instance, [{{IPA|nĩkrã}}] means 'wrist', while [{{IPA|nĩkra}}] means 'chair'. However, there is some variation in nasalization, and nasalization may spread to the left. [[Diphthong]]s also exist in Arikapú, and may contrast with two consecutive [[monophthong]]s, as in [{{IPA|kaj}}] 'head' versus [{{IPA|ka.i}}] 'hair'. Vowels may also become diphthongized in stressed syllables, with a {{IPAblink|j}} off-glide.<ref name="Voort2007"/>{{rp|137-138}}

==Writing system==
The Arikapú language is written using the same [[orthography]] as its [[sister language]], Djeoromitxí. It is based on applying the [[International Phonetic Alphabet]] to Arikapú's phonological system, with a few changes. The vowels /{{IPAlink|ə}}, {{IPAlink|ɛ}}, {{IPAlink|ɪ}}, {{IPAlink|ɔ}}, {{IPAlink|ɨ}}/ are written as {{angbr|ä, e, ï, o, ü}}, respectively. Nasalisation is indicated by a tilde on the vowel: {{angbr|ã ä̃ ẽ ĩ õ ũ}}. The consonants {{IPAslink|ʔ}} and {{IPAslink|t͡ʃ}} are written as {{angbr|'}} and {{angbr|tx}}. The writing system also writes out the predictable allophones as separate letters to reflect their actual pronunciation: underlying {{IPAslink|m}} is written as {{angbr|m}} or {{angbr|b}}, and underlying {{IPAslink|n}} is written as {{angbr|n}}, {{angbr|nd}}, or {{angbr|ndj}} depending on context.<ref name=Vocab/>{{rp|3}}

For alphabetization, the nasal marker {{angbr|˜}} is ignored, so {{angbr|a}} and {{angbr|ã}} are grouped together. The vowels with the {{angbr|¨}} diacritic are treated as separate letters, and are alphabetized immediately after their bare equivalents. The resulting alphabet has the following characters, in this order:<ref name=Vocab/>{{rp|3}}

==Morphosyntax==
Arikapú is an [[isolating language]], with a small set of obligatory personal prefixes. The functions of case marking are handled by postpositional modifiers/clitics that mark the semantic role of the arguments, with an [[Ergative–absolutive alignment|ergative]] marking structure. It has mostly [[free word order]], with a tendency toward [[Postpositive adjective|postnominal modifiers]] (Noun-Modifier order) and objects preceding the verb ([[Subject–object–verb word order|SOV]] or [[Object–verb–subject word order|OVS]] orders).<ref name=RV2010/>{{rp|525-526}}<ref name=Voort2007/>{{rp|139}}
